Longwinged
LONG-wingd
adj. (having long wings; of the great eagle in Ezekiel's riddle, which is Nebuchadnezzar)
English long + winged. At Ezekiel 17:3 it renders a Hebrew phrase meaning long of pinion — part of an unusually detailed description of a bird that stands for an empire.

Biblical Definition

Ezekiel is told to put forth a riddle and speak a parable, and it begins with a bird described in loving detail: Thus saith the Lord GOD; A great eagle with great wings, longwinged, full of feathers, which had divers colours, came unto Lebanon, and took the highest branch of the cedar. The reader is left to guess for nine verses, and then the interpretation is given plainly: Behold, the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem, and hath taken the king thereof, and the princes thereof, and led them with him to Babylon. The highest branch of the cedar is Jehoiachin; the second eagle is Egypt; and the vine that turns its roots toward the second eagle is Zedekiah, breaking the oath he had sworn to Nebuchadnezzar by the LORD.

The chapter is a sustained lesson in how to read Scripture's figures: the symbolism is dense, the interpretation is supplied by the text itself, and the point is a moral one. God's charge against Zedekiah is not politics but perjury — seeing he despised the oath by breaking the covenant — an oath sworn to a pagan emperor and binding because it was sworn in God's name. And the chapter ends with the LORD announcing that He will do what the eagles did, but for good: He will take of the highest branch of the high cedar and plant it upon a high mountain, and it shall bring forth boughs and bear fruit, and under it shall dwell all fowl of every wing.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): having long wings; in Scripture, of the great eagle of Ezekiel's parable.

expand to see more

LONG-WINGED, a. Having long wings; as a long-winged fowl.

EAGLE, n. A rapacious fowl of the genus Falco, remarkable for strength, size, flight and longevity.

PARABLE, n. A fable or allegorical relation of something real in life or nature, from which a moral is drawn.

RIDDLE, n. An enigma; something proposed for conjecture, or that is to be solved by conjecture.

CEDAR, n. A tree of the juniper or pine kind, of great size and durability.

Key Scripture

Ezekiel 17:3 — "And say, Thus saith the Lord GOD; A great eagle with great wings, longwinged, full of feathers, which had divers colours, came unto Lebanon, and took the highest branch of the cedar:"

Ezekiel 17:12 — "Say now to the rebellious house, Know ye not what these things mean? tell them, Behold, the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem, and hath taken the king thereof, and the princes thereof, and led them with him to Babylon;"

Jeremiah 4:13 — "Behold, he shall come up as clouds, and his chariots shall be as a whirlwind: his horses are swifter than eagles. Woe unto us! for we are spoiled."

Isaiah 40:31 — "But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint."

Modern Corruption

Prophetic symbolism is treated as infinitely pliable, when Ezekiel 17 is the model of the opposite — a figure whose meaning the text itself fixes, and fixes to a single historical event.

expand to see more

A great deal of prophetic interpretation proceeds as though symbols were free-floating, to be matched against whatever the interpreter finds in the newspaper. Ezekiel 17 is a rebuke to the method. The eagle, the cedar, the branch, the vine and the second eagle all mean something exact, and the prophet is made to say what: the king of Babylon, the king of Judah, Egypt, and an oath that was broken. The Reformed rule of interpretation follows this pattern — Scripture interprets Scripture, the plainer passages govern the obscurer, and a figure means what its own context says it means.

The moral at the centre also deserves recovery. Zedekiah's crime, as God states it, was breaking an oath he had sworn to Nebuchadnezzar — a pagan king, an occupying power — and the LORD treats it as a sin against Himself because the oath was sworn in His name. That is a high doctrine of the binding force of a promise. A Christian's word, given to an unbeliever, in a matter that has become inconvenient, is under the same rule: he sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not. And the chapter does not end in judgment. The last eagle is God, and what He plants on the high mountain bears fruit and shelters every wing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew arek ha-eber (H750 / H83), long of pinion; nesher (H5404), an eagle or great vulture; chidah (H2420), a riddle.

expand to see more

Hebrew eber (H83) — a pinion, a wing feather; joined to arek, long, for longwinged.

Hebrew nesher (H5404) — the eagle or great vulture; the empire in Ezekiel's riddle.

Hebrew chidah (H2420) — a riddle, a dark saying; what the prophet was told to put forth.

Hebrew mashal (H4912) — a parable, a proverb; the second term of the commission.

Hebrew alah (H423) — an oath, a curse; what Zedekiah despised by breaking the covenant.

Usage

"“A great eagle with great wings, longwinged, full of feathers” — a riddle with an exact answer."

"“Behold, the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem” — the answer supplied by the text."

"“under it shall dwell all fowl of every wing” — the last planting, and it is God's."
